solution: Use \(\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}\) with \(\tan A=\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}\). Numerator: \(\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}+\dfrac{n\sin A\cos A}{1-n\cos^2 A}=\dfrac{\sin A\left[(1-n\cos^2 A)+n\cos^2 A\right]}{\cos A\,(1-n\cos^2 A)}=\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A\,(1-n\cos^2 A)}\). Denominator: \(1-\dfrac{n\sin^2 A}{1-n\cos^2 A}=\dfrac{1-n\cos^2 A-n\sin^2 A}{1-n\cos^2 A}=\dfrac{1-n}{1-n\cos^2 A}\). Dividing, the factor \(1-n\cos^2 A\) cancels and \(\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{\sin A}{(1-n)\cos A}\). Verified numerically at \((n,A)=(3,0.5),\ (2.7,1.19),\ (-1.4,0.73),\ (5,0.31)\); the variants carrying \(n-1\) or \(n+1\) in the denominator disagree at every one of them. Matches option A.

\[\text{Dr} = 1-\dfrac{n\sin^2 A}{1-n\cos^2 A} = \dfrac{1-n\cos^2 A-n\sin^2 A}{1-n\cos^2 A} = \dfrac{1-n}{1-n\cos^2 A}\]

The numerator is \(2\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\cos 10^\circ-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin 10^\circ\right)=2\left(\cos 60^\circ\cos 10^\circ-\sin 60^\circ\sin 10^\circ\right)=2\cos 70^\circ=2\sin 20^\circ\), and the denominator is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\sin 20^\circ\). Hence the value is \(\dfrac{2\sin 20^\circ}{\tfrac{1}{2}\sin 20^\circ}=4\), confirmed numerically as \(4.000\ldots\) to 25 decimal places. Since \(4\) is a positive integer it is a natural number; it is therefore not a surd, not non-integral, and not negative. Matches option D.

solution: Put \(y=30^\circ-x\). Then \(\cot x=\tan(90^\circ-x)=\tan(60^\circ+y)\), \(\cot(60^\circ+x)=\tan(30^\circ-x)=\tan y\), and \(\cot(120^\circ+x)=\tan(-30^\circ-x)=\tan(y-60^\circ)=\tan(y+120^\circ)\) by the period \(180^\circ\). So the sum is \(\tan y+\tan(y+60^\circ)+\tan(y+120^\circ)=3\tan 3y\), and \(3y=90^\circ-3x\) gives \(\tan 3y=\cot 3x\). Hence the sum equals \(3\cot 3x\). Substituting \(\tan 3x=\dfrac{3\tan x-\tan^3 x}{1-3\tan^2 x}\) gives \(3\cot 3x=\dfrac{3-9\tan^2 x}{3\tan x-\tan^3 x}\), which is the printed form. Numerical check at \(x=10^\circ,\ 17.3^\circ,\ 41.9^\circ,\ 7.1^\circ\) matches that form exactly. Note that the bare value \(\tan 3x\) agrees only by coincidence at \(x=20^\circ\), where \(3\cot 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}=\tan 60^\circ\): at \(x=10^\circ\) the sum is \(5.19615\) while \(\tan 3x=0.57735\). The value \(\cot 3x\) is out by a factor of \(3\). Matches option D.

solution: Use \(1-\sin x=\left(\sin\frac{x}{2}-\cos\frac{x}{2}\right)^2\) and \(1+\sin x=\left(\sin\frac{x}{2}+\cos\frac{x}{2}\right)^2\). For \(\frac{5\pi}{2}<x<3\pi\) we have \(\frac{x}{2}\in\left(\frac{5\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)\), a third-quadrant angle in which \(\left|\sin\frac{x}{2}\right|\ge\left|\cos\frac{x}{2}\right|\); hence \(\sin\frac{x}{2}<0\), \(\cos\frac{x}{2}<0\), \(\sin\frac{x}{2}-\cos\frac{x}{2}\le 0\) and \(\sin\frac{x}{2}+\cos\frac{x}{2}<0\). Taking the positive square roots, \(\sqrt{1-\sin x}=\cos\frac{x}{2}-\sin\frac{x}{2}\) and \(\sqrt{1+\sin x}=-\left(\sin\frac{x}{2}+\cos\frac{x}{2}\right)\). The numerator becomes \(-2\sin\frac{x}{2}\) and the denominator \(2\cos\frac{x}{2}\), so the expression is \(-\tan\frac{x}{2}\). Checked at \(x=2.55\pi,\ 2.6\pi,\ 2.75\pi,\ 2.9\pi,\ 2.99\pi\): the expression is negative throughout and equals \(-\tan\frac{x}{2}\) exactly, whereas \(\tan\frac{x}{2}\) has the wrong sign and both cotangent forms have the wrong magnitude. Matches option D.

solution: Pair the terms. From \(\cot\theta-\tan\theta=2\cot 2\theta\), \(\cot 7\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ-\tan 7\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ=2\cot 15^\circ=2\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)=4+2\sqrt{3}\). From \(\tan\theta-\cot\theta=-2\cot 2\theta\), \(\tan 67\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ-\cot 67\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ=-2\cot 135^\circ=2\). The total is \(6+2\sqrt{3}=2\left(3+\sqrt{3}\right)\approx 9.4641016\), confirmed numerically to 25 decimal places. That value is irrational, so it is not a rational number; and as printed, \(2\left(3+2\sqrt{3}\right)\approx 12.9282\) and \(2\left(3-\sqrt{3}\right)\approx 2.5359\) are both different from it. The only statement that is true of the value is that it is irrational. Matches option B.

solution: \(\cos 4\theta=1-2\sin^2 2\theta\), so \(x+y=3-\cos 4\theta=2+2\sin^2 2\theta\) while \(x-y=4\sin 2\theta\). Adding and subtracting, \(x=1+2\sin 2\theta+\sin^2 2\theta=\left(1+\sin 2\theta\right)^2\) and \(y=1-2\sin 2\theta+\sin^2 2\theta=\left(1-\sin 2\theta\right)^2\). Since \(\left|\sin 2\theta\right|\le 1\), both bases are non-negative, so the positive square roots are \(\sqrt{x}=1+\sin 2\theta\) and \(\sqrt{y}=1-\sin 2\theta\), giving \(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=2\) for every \(\theta\). Checked at \(\theta=0.31,\ 0.73,\ 1.19,\ 2.4,\ -0.5\): \(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=2\) every time and never \(16\), whereas \(x^4+y^4\) takes the values \(39.04,\ 249.79,\ 66.57,\ 252.10,\ 132.23\) and so is not the constant \(9\), and \(x^3+y^3\ne 2\left(x^2+y^2\right)\) at any of them. Matches option D.

solution: Expanding the tangent of a three-term sum, \(\tan(A+B+C)=\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B+\tan C-\tan A\tan B\tan C}{1-\left(\tan A\tan B+\tan B\tan C+\tan C\tan A\right)}\). The given relation makes the numerator vanish, so \(\tan(A+B+C)=0\) and \(A+B+C\) is an integral multiple of \(\pi\). The degenerate case in which the denominator vanishes as well cannot occur over the reals: writing \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) for the elementary symmetric functions of \(\tan A,\tan B,\tan C\), the two conditions \(e_1=e_3\) and \(e_2=1\) turn the cubic \(z^3-e_1z^2+e_2z-e_3\) into \(\left(z-e_1\right)\left(z^2+1\right)\), whose only real root is \(z=e_1\); all three tangents are then equal to \(e_1=3\tan A\), which forces \(\tan A=0\) and contradicts \(e_2=1\). Being the angles of a triangle is only the case \(n=1\) and so is not forced, and requiring the sum of two of the angles to equal the third would force all three to vanish. Numerically the relation holds exactly for sums \(0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ -\pi\) and fails (residual \(2.326\)) for a sum of \(2.04\). Matches option C.

The denominator cannot vanish at the same time over the reals: writing \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) for the elementary symmetric functions of the three tangents, \(e_1=e_3\) and \(e_2=1\) turn \(z^3-e_1z^2+e_2z-e_3\) into \(\left(z-e_1\right)\left(z^2+1\right)\), whose only real root is \(z=e_1\); all three tangents are then equal to \(e_1=3\tan A\), which forces \(\tan A=0\) and contradicts \(e_2=1\).
Hence the sum of the three angles is an integral multiple of \(\pi\).

solution: Since \(\sin 3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3 x\), for \(x\ne n\pi\) we get \(f(x)=\dfrac{\sin 3x}{\sin x}=3-4\sin^2 x\). Here \(\sin^2 x\) runs over \((0,1]\): it equals \(1\) at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\), but it can never equal \(0\) precisely because \(x\ne n\pi\) is excluded. Hence \(f\) attains its least value \(3-4=-1\), and rises towards \(3\) as \(\sin^2 x\to 0\) without ever reaching it. The range is therefore \([-1,3)\), closed at the lower end and open at the upper. A dense scan of \((0,\pi)\) returns a minimum of exactly \(-1\) and values climbing to \(2.999999999\) while never attaining \(3\), which rules out the closed interval \([-1,3]\). Matches option D.

solution: Use \(\cos^2\theta+3\sin^2\theta=1+2\sin^2\theta=2-\cos 2\theta\) and \(6\sin\theta\cos\theta=3\sin 2\theta\). The expression becomes \(2-\cos 2\theta-3\sin 2\theta+2=4-\left(\cos 2\theta+3\sin 2\theta\right)\). Since \(a\cos\phi+b\sin\phi\) ranges over \(\left[-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\ \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right]\), here \(\cos 2\theta+3\sin 2\theta\in\left[-\sqrt{10},\ \sqrt{10}\right]\), so the expression ranges over \(\left[4-\sqrt{10},\ 4+\sqrt{10}\right]\) and its minimum is \(4-\sqrt{10}\approx 0.8377223\). A dense scan over a full period returns \(0.8377223\); note \(4+\sqrt{10}\) is the maximum, not the minimum, and the value never reaches \(0\). Matches option B.

Convert to cosines: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{14}=\cos\frac{3\pi}{7}\), \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{14}=\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}\), \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{14}=\cos\frac{\pi}{7}\), and \(\cos\frac{3\pi}{7}=-\cos\frac{4\pi}{7}\). The product therefore equals \(-\cos\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}\cos\frac{4\pi}{7}\). By the doubling identity \(\cos\alpha\cos 2\alpha\cos 4\alpha=\dfrac{\sin 8\alpha}{8\sin\alpha}\) with \(\alpha=\frac{\pi}{7}\), that triple product is \(\dfrac{\sin\frac{8\pi}{7}}{8\sin\frac{\pi}{7}}=\dfrac{-\sin\frac{\pi}{7}}{8\sin\frac{\pi}{7}}=-\dfrac{1}{8}\). Hence the required value is \(\dfrac{1}{8}\), confirmed numerically as \(0.125\) to 25 decimal places, which rules out \(\frac{1}{16}=0.0625\). Matches option B.
